turns.human_input: We built a B2B project management tool for construction companies. It's been 14 months, we have 23 paying customers, $180K ARR, but growth has stalled for four months. In our last ten sales calls, seven prospects said they actually wanted the workflow automation piece more than the project tracking. My co-founder thinks we should pivot to a workflow automation platform for construction. I'm less sure. What are the factors we should be weighing?
turns.ai_response:
This is a classic signal-versus-noise problem in early-stage product strategy. Here are the factors that actually matter.

On the signal side: seven out of ten is not a small sample. When prospects consistently tell you what they wish you were, that's directional even if it's not statistically robust. The fact that it's coming up in active sales calls — where people have a reason to pay attention — makes it stronger than survey data. And if the workflow automation request is coming from the same construction persona you already sell to, the market access cost of a pivot is lower than starting from scratch.

On the risk side: you have 23 paying customers who bought you as a project management tool. A pivot changes your product roadmap, potentially your messaging, and raises a real question about what happens to their contracts and expectations. There's also the question of whether 'workflow automation for construction' is a sharper product or just a broader promise — automation is often harder to scope cleanly than tracking.

The question I'd push on first: when those seven prospects said they wanted workflow automation, did they describe a specific workflow? Or did they use it as a general expression of wanting more power? There's a meaningful difference between 'I need permit approval workflows automated' and 'I want more automation.' The former is a product spec; the latter is a sentiment.

Also worth separating: is this a pivot away from project management, or an extension into automation that lives alongside it? The latter is often more viable than a full pivot.

turns.human_input: The prospects were pretty specific — they mentioned RFI workflows, subcontractor approval chains, and permit tracking as the main pain points. We've been going back and forth internally for six weeks and I'm paralyzed. My co-founder wants a decision this week. What would you do?
turns.ai_response:
Given those specifics, I'd move toward the pivot — but not as a full platform rewrite. Here's what I'd actually do.

RFI workflows, subcontractor approvals, and permit tracking are not abstract automation wishes. They're named pain points that construction teams deal with daily and that carry real cost when they're slow or manual. That specificity is meaningful. It means you're not chasing a vague market segment; you're being pulled toward a concrete feature set by people who have already shown willingness to pay in your existing category.

The move I'd make: commit to a focused automation module — not a platform pivot — targeted at one of those three workflows. Pick the one that overlaps most with data you already collect in your project management tool. RFI workflows are probably the closest to project tracking and the least likely to require starting from scratch architecturally.

Build it for two to three of your existing customers first. Get paid for it. If it holds up, you have a wedge to expand the automation surface and a story that says 'we started in project management and moved into construction workflow automation,' which is a credible evolution rather than a distress pivot.

This also resolves the internal conflict: you're not betting the existing $180K ARR on a full rewrite. You're running a contained experiment that your co-founder's instinct supports and that your caution can accept.

The six-week paralysis is the real cost here. Make the decision to run the experiment this week, not the decision to pivot wholesale.

turns.human_input: We started building the RFI workflow module two weeks ago. Our three largest customers are beta testing it. But yesterday one of them said they'd pay $800/month for just the RFI workflow tool on its own — twice what they pay now for the full project management suite. That changes things. Does it?
turns.ai_response:
Yes, it changes things meaningfully — but in a specific way.

One customer expressing willingness to pay twice as much is a strong signal but not a decision. What it tells you is that the perceived value of the automation module is high enough to command premium pricing independent of the broader suite. That's the important part. It means you may not need the project management product as a bundling mechanism to justify the price.

What it doesn't tell you: whether the other two beta customers feel the same way, whether 'would pay' converts to 'will pay' when you actually invoice them, and whether the $800/month figure is anchored to their specific pain or to a competitive comparison they're making.

The question this raises for your strategy: are you building a module to add to your existing product, or are you discovering that the automation piece is actually the primary product and the project management suite has been holding back your pricing? If it's the latter, the full pivot your co-founder originally proposed deserves a more serious look — not as abandonment of existing customers, but as a repositioning of what you are.

I'd run a quick test before drawing conclusions: ask all three beta customers the same direct question — 'If this RFI workflow tool were a standalone product at $800/month, would you buy it separately from the project management suite?' The answer distribution across three customers will tell you more than any single data point.

turns.human_input: All three said yes. Two of them said they'd actually prefer to drop the project management suite and just pay for the workflow automation. I've thought about this a lot over the past 24 hours and I've made my decision: we're doing the full pivot. I'm not second-guessing it. What I need now is help thinking through how to manage the transition with existing customers who are on the project management product.
turns.ai_response:
Good — here's how to handle the transition without burning the relationships you've built.

The core principle: give existing customers a clear path, a generous timeline, and no surprises. The customers most likely to stay through a pivot are your best customers, so treat this as a retention and upgrade conversation, not an offboarding conversation.

For customers who want both products during a transition period, offer a bundled rate that locks them into the automation product at a preferential price in exchange for a 12-month commitment. This converts them from at-risk churners into early automation customers with upside for you.

For customers who only want the project management product and have no interest in automation, be direct. Give them a sunset date — no less than 6 months out, ideally 12 — and help them find alternatives if needed. The cost of maintaining a zombie product for a small cohort of legacy customers is higher than the cost of graceful offboarding.

Practically: segment your 23 customers into three buckets right now — automation-ready (likely to upgrade), undecided (need a conversation), and legacy-only (likely to churn). That segmentation tells you where to spend your transition energy.

One operational note: don't announce the pivot publicly until you've had individual conversations with your top 5 accounts. They should hear it from you before they read it anywhere.

turns.human_input: We've started the customer conversations. Most are going well. But now my co-founder and I disagree on pricing for the new automation product. I want to start at $500/month to make adoption easy. She wants to start at $1200/month based on the value the beta customers described. We both have arguments. Can we think through the pricing decision together?
turns.ai_response:
Let's work through both positions and see what the evidence actually supports.

Your $500 case: lower entry price reduces friction for new customers who haven't used the product yet, accelerates early adoption data, and keeps you competitive if other tools enter the space. It leaves room to raise prices once you have a stronger track record and more case studies. The risk is anchoring your market at a lower price point that's hard to move up from — early customers often resist price increases even when value has been demonstrated.

Her $1200 case: your beta customers told you they'd pay $800/month for the RFI module alone, before you had a finished product and before you had customer success stories. $1200 for a complete workflow automation suite is arguably a natural extension of that signal. Starting high lets you discount selectively and test price sensitivity without permanently setting a floor. The risk is that a $1200 price point early in your sales motion, before you have clear ROI benchmarks, creates unnecessary friction in deals.

The synthesis I'd push you toward: start at $900/month for your first ten post-pivot customers with an explicit early-adopter framing. This is above your hesitation point but below her target, and it comes with a rationale — early customers get a better price in exchange for feedback and case study rights. It also gives you a clear comparison point: when those ten deals close or don't, you'll have real conversion data to set the steady-state price.

What matters most is picking a number you can both commit to executing on. A split team on pricing shows up in sales conversations.
